question: What is the MVC design pattern and why does it exist?
title: Spring MVC & REST
direct_answer: MVC separates request coordination, application/domain work, and presentation. In Spring MVC, DispatcherServlet handles requests mapped to it, selects a handler, and then renders a view or writes a response body. It does not receive literally every HTTP request before filters or other servlets. @RestController applies response-body semantics, and converters—not the annotation itself—produce JSON, XML, text, or other supported formats.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the MVC separation of concerns, the role of DispatcherServlet in Spring MVC, and how @RestController differs from @Controller.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting business logic in controller methods, or not understanding that @RestController implies @ResponseBody for all methods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the request lifecycle in Spring MVC (DispatcherServlet -> HandlerMapping -> Controller -> ViewResolver or MessageConverter), and how content negotiation chooses JSON vs XML.

sections.title: MVC and Spring's Request Pipeline
sections.content:
The servlet request path is filters -> DispatcherServlet -> handler mapping/adapter -> controller -> return-value handling. Exceptions can be handled by MVC resolvers or the container/Boot error path.

For REST, the 'view' is not simply JSON as a template; response-body processing is a separate MVC return path. Keep HTTP DTOs separate from persistence entities when that protects the contract, but avoid mapping layers that add no value to a trivial bounded endpoint.

**Example.** GET /orders/42 reaches DispatcherServlet, which finds an @GetMapping method. The controller calls a service, returns an OrderResponse, and an HTTP message converter writes that object as JSON; a view controller instead returns a model and view name.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Controller handles HTTP input/output coordination.
Model/domain/service code represents data and business behavior.
View rendering is one output path; message conversion is another.
Filters and servlet mapping exist outside/before DispatcherServlet handling.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A page controller can add OrderDto to Model and return a Thymeleaf view name. An API controller can return OrderDto from @RestController; MVC then chooses a converter for the negotiated media type. In both cases the controller should delegate business rules to an appropriate application/service boundary. MVC is a separation pattern, not a requirement to create an empty layer for every operation.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The DispatcherServlet is the front controller that receives every HTTP request and orchestrates the entire MVC workflow. HandlerMapping maps URL patterns to controller methods based on @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping annotations. @Controller marks a class as a web controller whose methods return view names; @RestController adds @ResponseBody to every method so return values are serialized directly to the response body. @RequestBody binds the HTTP request body to a Java object via Jackson deserialization, while @ResponseBody serializes the return value to JSON or XML. @PathVariable extracts values from URL templates like /tasks/{id}, and @RequestParam extracts query-string parameters. The service layer holds business logic and transaction boundaries; the controller should be thin, delegating to services. ViewResolver resolves logical view names to physical templates (Thymeleaf, JSP) for server-rendered pages, while MessageConverter handles JSON/XML serialization for REST endpoints.

sections.title: Spring REST Controller with CRUD Endpoints
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: MVC enforces a clean separation between presentation and business logic, making controllers testable and views swappable, but it adds layers that can feel heavy for simple CRUD APIs where the controller directly returns a DTO. Spring's auto-configuration makes it trivial to set up a REST controller, but the implicit magic (content negotiation, exception handling, serialization) can be hard to debug when something goes wrong. For REST APIs specifically, @RestController is preferred over @Controller because it eliminates the unnecessary view-resolution step. Putting business logic in controllers is the most common anti-pattern -- controllers should be thin, delegating to services that manage transactions and domain rules.

question: What is the MVC design pattern?
title: MVC Pattern Explained — Model, View, Controller
direct_answer: MVC (Model-View-Controller) is an architectural pattern that separates an application into three components: Model (data and business logic), View (presentation/UI), and Controller (handles HTTP requests, coordinates model and view). It promotes separation of concerns.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of fundamental architectural pattern separation and its purpose in web applications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking MVC is Spring-specific or just naming the three layers without explaining why separation matters
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how Spring MVC implements this pattern with DispatcherServlet as front controller and show real request flow

sections.title: Understanding MVC Architecture
sections.content:
**MVC (Model-View-Controller)** is a design pattern from the 1970s that divides application logic into three interconnected parts.

Think of it like a restaurant: the **Controller** is the waiter who takes your order (HTTP request), the **Model** is the kitchen that prepares food (business logic and data), and the **View** is the plated dish presented to you (HTML/JSON response). This separation means you can change how food is plated without retraining waiters or redesigning the kitchen.

In Spring Boot REST APIs, **Controller** handles incoming requests, **Model** represents domain objects and business rules, and **View** is typically JSON serialization. The pattern prevents mixing concerns — no database queries in presentation code, no HTML generation in business logic. Each layer has a single responsibility and can evolve independently.

sections.title: The Three MVC Components
sections.content:
amber|Model|~Data + business logic|domain objects, services|knows nothing about HTTP|the what
blue|View|~Presentation layer|Thymeleaf/JSP or JSON|renders the response|the look
emerald|Controller|~Coordinator|handles HTTP request|calls model, picks view|the glue
violet|Why MVC|~Separation of concerns|each layer one job|easier to test + change|less coupling

sections.title: MVC Pattern in Spring Boot REST API
When to Use MVC Pattern
sections.content:
Use MVC in **web applications** where you need clear separation between user interaction, business rules, and data handling. It's ideal for **Spring Boot REST APIs** where controllers map HTTP endpoints, services contain order processing or payment logic, and repositories handle database access.

Apply MVC when building **multi-page applications with Thymeleaf** where views are HTML templates, or **mobile backends** where views are JSON responses. The pattern shines when multiple developers work on different layers simultaneously — frontend team modifies views, backend team changes business logic, without stepping on each other's code.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Fat Controllers**: Learners put business logic directly in controller methods — calculating totals, validating rules, querying databases. Controllers should only handle HTTP concerns (parsing request, returning response) and delegate to services.
- **Skipping Service Layer**: Calling repository methods directly from controllers because it's fewer lines of code. This scatters business logic across controllers and makes testing harder.
- **Mixing View Logic**: Building JSON strings manually or formatting data in controllers instead of using dedicated response DTOs. Let Jackson handle serialization and keep controllers thin.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Model**: Domain objects (Order, User) and business logic in service classes, represents application state and rules
**View**: Presentation layer — JSON responses in REST APIs via Jackson serialization, or HTML templates in traditional web apps
**Controller**: Handles HTTP requests, extracts parameters, calls service methods, returns responses — no business logic here
**DispatcherServlet**: Spring's front controller that routes incoming requests to appropriate controller methods based on URL mappings
**Separation of Concerns**: Each layer has single responsibility, changes to one layer don't force changes in others

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: MVC is a design pattern that splits your application into three parts: Model, View, and Controller. It's been around since the seventies and isn't specific to Spring. The Controller handles incoming HTTP requests — it's like a waiter taking orders. The Model contains your business logic and data — that's the kitchen preparing food. The View is what gets sent back to the client — the plated dish. In a Spring Boot REST API, the Controller is your @RestController class that maps URLs. The Model is your service layer with business rules and your domain objects like Order or Customer. The View is usually JSON that Jackson creates from your response objects. The whole point is separation of concerns. You don't put database queries in your controller. You don't write business logic in your view. Each layer does one thing well. If you need to change how orders are validated, you only touch the service class. If you need to add a new endpoint, you only touch the controller. This makes the code easier to test because you can test business logic without spinning up a web server. Spring implements this with DispatcherServlet as the front controller that routes requests to your methods. A common mistake is putting everything in the controller — that's called a fat controller and it breaks the pattern. Keep controllers thin, they should just coordinate between the request and your service layer.

question: What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?
title: @Controller vs @RestController in Spring MVC
direct_answer: @Controller marks a Spring MVC controller; its methods can render views or write response bodies. @RestController combines @Controller with class-level @ResponseBody, so its handler return values are written through HttpMessageConverters by default. JSON is common but not required. A @Controller method can also return data by adding @ResponseBody or ResponseEntity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring's composed annotations and the difference between traditional MVC and RESTful responses
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Controller for REST endpoints and forgetting @ResponseBody on every method, causing view resolution errors
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @RestController is a meta-annotation combining @Controller and @ResponseBody, and describe Jackson's role

sections.title: @Controller and @RestController
sections.content:
Both annotations create controller beans and use the same request mapping, argument binding, validation, and exception-resolution infrastructure. @RestController is a convenience meta-annotation.

When a method returns String, context matters: in a normal @Controller it is often a view name; under response-body handling it is usually literal body text. ResponseEntity always represents an HTTP response and can be returned from either controller style.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: @Controller does not force every return value to be a view name.
@RestController applies response-body handling to all handler methods.
Message converters can write JSON, XML, text, bytes, resources, and other supported formats.
Choose based on the class's dominant response style.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A Thymeleaf controller can return the view name orders and add data to Model. An API controller can return OrderDto from @RestController and let a converter write the negotiated representation. A mixed @Controller can use ordinary view-returning methods and add @ResponseBody on a health or download method. The distinction is return-value handling, not 'Controller always HTML and RestController always Jackson JSON'.

sections.title: @Controller vs @RestController
sections.content:
amber|@Controller|~Returns a view name|String to ViewResolver|renders an HTML page|server-side MVC
blue|@RestController|~@Controller + @ResponseBody|return object to JSON|no view resolution|REST APIs
emerald|@ResponseBody|~The deciding piece|serialize via converter|skips ViewResolver|implicit in @RestController
rose|Common trap|~@RestController returns String|treated as raw body text|not a view name|you see literal text

sections.title: @Controller vs @RestController in Code
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **@Controller** when building traditional multi-page web applications with **Thymeleaf** or **JSP** where you render HTML on the server. Your methods return view names and Spring resolves them to template files.

Use **@RestController** for **REST APIs** consumed by frontend frameworks (React, Angular) or mobile apps. Every method returns a Java object that Jackson automatically serializes to JSON. If you're building a Spring Boot backend that only serves JSON endpoints and has no server-side HTML rendering, always use @RestController. If you have one or two REST endpoints in a mostly-HTML application, you can use @Controller with @ResponseBody on those specific methods.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting @ResponseBody**: Using @Controller for REST endpoints and not adding @ResponseBody to methods. Spring tries to resolve the returned object as a view name, resulting in "template not found" errors. You see 404s or "Could not resolve view" exceptions.
- **Mixing Annotations**: Using @RestController but trying to return view names — doesn't work because @ResponseBody is applied to all methods.
- **Not Understanding Jackson**: Freshers don't realize @RestController triggers automatic JSON serialization. They manually build JSON strings or use ObjectMapper explicitly when Jackson does it automatically for POJOs.

question: What is separation of concerns in MVC?
title: Separation of Concerns in MVC — Why It Matters
direct_answer: Separation of concerns in MVC means each layer has a single, well-defined responsibility: Controller handles HTTP, Service handles business logic, Repository handles data access, View handles presentation. No business logic in controllers or views — each layer can change independently.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of why layered architecture matters beyond just memorizing layer names
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting business logic in controllers (fat controllers) or mixing data access code with HTTP handling
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe concrete examples of what code belongs in each layer and why breaking separation causes maintenance problems

sections.title: Separation of Concerns Principle
sections.content:
**Separation of concerns** means dividing your application so each part has one clear job and doesn't overlap with others.

Think of it like a hospital: reception handles check-in paperwork (Controller), doctors diagnose and treat (Service with business logic), lab technicians run tests (Repository accessing database), and the billing department formats invoices (View). If the receptionist started diagnosing patients, chaos ensues.

In Spring MVC, **Controllers** only handle HTTP — parsing request parameters, calling service methods, returning responses. **Services** contain all business rules — validating orders, calculating discounts, orchestrating workflows. **Repositories** only talk to the database — no business logic here. **Views** (or DTOs in REST) only format data for presentation. When each layer respects its boundary, you can change database structure without touching controllers, or add new validation rules without modifying HTTP handling.

sections.title: Layers and Their Single Responsibility
sections.content:
amber|Controller|~HTTP boundary|parse request, validate|return response|no business logic
blue|Service|~Business logic|transactions, rules|reusable, testable|no HTTP types
emerald|Repository|~Data access|JPA / SQL queries|persistence only|no business rules
violet|Why split|~Single responsibility|swap a layer safely|unit test in isolation|clean architecture

sections.title: Proper Separation of Concerns
When Separation of Concerns Matters
sections.content:
Apply strict separation when building **enterprise applications** with complex business rules — pricing calculations, multi-step workflows, integration with external services. It's critical in **team environments** where different developers own different layers and need clear contracts between them.

Use this discipline in **long-lived codebases** that will be maintained for years — proper separation prevents the codebase from turning into a tangled mess where changing one thing breaks three others. Even in small projects, separating concerns from day one prevents the **big ball of mud** anti-pattern where everything is coupled and refactoring becomes impossible.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Fat Controllers**: Learners put validation, calculations, and database queries directly in controller methods because it seems faster. You end up with 200-line controller methods full of business logic. This makes unit testing impossible without starting the web layer.
- **Service Layer Bypass**: Calling repository methods directly from controllers to save typing. Then you have the same business logic duplicated across multiple controllers.
- **Business Logic in Repositories**: Writing complex queries with joins and aggregations in repository methods and considering that "business logic". Repositories should be thin data access — complex calculations belong in services.
- **Mixing Concerns**: Formatting dates or building error messages in service layer, or validating data in controllers. Each layer should do its job and nothing else.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Controller Layer**: Handles HTTP requests and responses — parameter extraction, status codes, exception mapping to HTTP errors, no business logic
**Service Layer**: Contains all business logic — validation rules, calculations, workflow orchestration, transaction boundaries with @Transactional
**Repository Layer**: Data access only — queries, inserts, updates, deletes using JPA or JDBC, no business rules or calculations
**View/DTO Layer**: Data transfer objects for API responses, formatted for client needs, no logic beyond simple field mapping
**Single Responsibility**: Each class and method has one reason to change, controller changes for new endpoints, service for new business rules

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Separation of concerns means each layer in your application has one clear job and doesn't do someone else's work. In Spring MVC, the Controller layer handles HTTP stuff — it takes in request parameters, calls the service, and returns a response with the right status code. That's it. No business logic here. The Service layer is where all your business rules live. If you're validating that an order total is positive, or calculating shipping costs, or checking inventory before confirming an order, that's all in the service. The Repository layer only talks to the database — it runs queries and returns data, nothing more. And your DTOs or response objects just format data for the client. Why does this matter? Because it makes your code way easier to maintain and test. If I need to add a new validation rule, I only touch the service class. If I need to change the database query, I only touch the repository. I can unit test my business logic without starting a web server or connecting to a database because the service doesn't know about HTTP. A huge mistake Learners make is putting business logic in controllers — that's called a fat controller. You'll see controller methods that are 200 lines long with calculations and database calls mixed in. That's impossible to test and a nightmare to change later. Another mistake is calling repositories directly from controllers to save time. Then you end up duplicating the same business logic across multiple controllers. Always put business logic in services, keep controllers thin, and let repositories just handle data access. That's proper separation of concerns.

question: What is @RequestMapping in Spring MVC?
title: @RequestMapping in Spring MVC — URL Mapping and HTTP Methods
direct_answer: @RequestMapping maps HTTP requests to controller methods or classes. At the class level it sets the base URL path; at the method level it refines with sub-path and HTTP method. Shorthand annotations @GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc., are composites of @RequestMapping.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of Spring MVC request routing and URL mapping annotations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verbose @RequestMapping with method parameter instead of shorthand annotations like @GetMapping
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how class-level and method-level mappings combine, and show awareness of composed annotations

sections.title: Understanding Request Mapping
sections.content:
**@RequestMapping** is Spring MVC's core annotation for routing HTTP requests to controller methods. It tells Spring's **DispatcherServlet** which method should handle requests to a specific URL path and HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE).

You can apply it at the **class level** to set a base path for all methods in that controller — like "/api/users" — and then at the **method level** to add sub-paths — like "/{id}" or "/search". Spring combines them: class "/api/users" + method "/{id}" becomes "/api/users/{id}". You can specify HTTP methods with the method attribute, but Spring provides shorthand annotations: **@GetMapping**, **@PostMapping**, **@PutMapping**, **@DeleteMapping**, **@PatchMapping**. These are cleaner and more idiomatic than writing @RequestMapping(method=RequestMethod.GET). Think of @RequestMapping as the generic version and the others as specialized shortcuts.

sections.title: @RequestMapping at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Class level|~Base path|@RequestMapping("/api")|shared by all methods|sets the prefix
blue|Method level|~Refines the route|sub-path + HTTP method|@GetMapping("/{id}")|final URL = prefix + sub
emerald|Shortcuts|~Per HTTP verb|@GetMapping, @PostMapping|@PutMapping, @DeleteMapping|since Spring 4.3
rose|Attributes|~Narrow the match|produces, consumes|params, headers|content negotiation

sections.title: RequestMapping Examples
When to Use Request Mapping
sections.content:
Use **@RequestMapping** at the class level to group related endpoints under a common base path — all customer operations under "/api/customers", all order operations under "/api/orders".

Use the HTTP-specific shortcuts (**@GetMapping**, **@PostMapping**) at the method level for individual operations — they're more readable than @RequestMapping(method=GET).

Use path variables with **{id}** or **{code}** when the resource identifier is part of the URL structure.

Use query parameters (via @RequestParam) for optional filters or search criteria.

Apply @RequestMapping directly at method level without class-level mapping when you have standalone endpoints that don't fit a resource pattern, though this is rare in REST APIs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Verbose Syntax**: Writing @RequestMapping(value="/users", method=RequestMethod.GET) instead of @GetMapping("/users"). The shorthand is standard in modern Spring Boot and more readable.
- **Missing Class-Level Path**: Repeating the full path in every method — @GetMapping("/api/users") in ten methods instead of @RequestMapping("/api/users") once at class level. This makes refactoring paths painful.
- **Forgetting Path Variables**: Declaring a path template like "/{id}" but not extracting it with @PathVariable in the method signature. Spring can't match the request because the parameter isn't bound.
- **Ambiguous Mappings**: Creating two methods with the same path and HTTP method — Spring throws an error at startup because it can't decide which method to call.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **@RequestMapping**: Core annotation for mapping HTTP requests to controller methods, works at class or method level
**Class-Level Mapping**: Sets base path for all methods in controller, like @RequestMapping("/api/orders") applies to entire class
**Method-Level Mapping**: Adds sub-path and HTTP method specifics, combined with class path to form full route
**Path Variables**: Placeholder in URL like /{id} extracted with @PathVariable annotation in method parameter
**Shorthand Annotations**: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping are cleaner than @RequestMapping(method=...)

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @RequestMapping is how you tell Spring which controller method should handle a specific HTTP request. You can use it at the class level to set a base path for all your endpoints. For example, if you put @RequestMapping with "/api/orders" on the class, that becomes the prefix for every method inside. Then at the method level, you add sub-paths and specify the HTTP method. But here's the thing — nobody uses @RequestMapping with the method parameter anymore. Spring gives you shorthand annotations: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping. These are way cleaner and they're actually composed annotations that wrap @RequestMapping internally. So @GetMapping is just shorthand for @RequestMapping with method equals GET. In practice, you'd have @RequestMapping on the class with your base path, then @GetMapping, @PostMapping on individual methods. Spring combines them — if your class has "/api/orders" and your method has "/{id}", the full path is "/api/orders/{id}". You extract that id parameter using @PathVariable in your method signature. A common mistake is writing the old verbose style — @RequestMapping with value and method parameters on every method. That's outdated Spring 2 style. Modern Spring Boot uses the shorthand annotations. Another mistake is not using class-level mapping and repeating the full path in every method. Then if you need to change the base path, you're editing ten methods instead of one line.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @RequestMapping is the base annotation in Spring MVC for routing HTTP requests to controller methods. You put it on the class to define a base path like /api/users, then on each method to specify the sub-path and HTTP verb.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: @GetMapping — read a resource, maps HTTP GET
@PostMapping — create a resource, maps HTTP POST
@PutMapping — replace a resource fully, maps HTTP PUT
@PatchMapping — update a resource partially, maps HTTP PATCH
@DeleteMapping — remove a resource, maps HTTP DELETE

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: These shorthand annotations are just @RequestMapping with the HTTP method already set. They're the modern idiomatic style — you'd only use bare @RequestMapping when you need to match multiple methods or set produces and consumes constraints.

beats.label: example
beats.content: A class annotated with @RequestMapping of /api/users and a method with @GetMapping of /{id} handles GET /api/users/123. Spring concatenates the class path and method path automatically.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: non-obvious: The produces attribute restricts which content types the endpoint returns, and consumes restricts which content types it accepts. If a client sends a content type that doesn't match consumes, Spring returns 415 Unsupported Media Type before your method is even called.

speakable_v2.cap: In practice: @RequestMapping on the class for the base path, then @GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc. on each method. That's the standard style.

question: What is the Model in Spring MVC?
title: Model in Spring MVC — Passing Data from Controller to View
direct_answer: In Spring MVC, Model is a holder for attributes exposed to a view during server-side rendering. A controller adds values and returns a view name; the selected view reads those attributes. A Java object returned from a @RestController is not 'the Model' in this sense—it is a handler return value written to the response body by an HttpMessageConverter.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Spring MVC passes data from controller layer to presentation layer and the distinction between Model interface vs MVC pattern's Model layer
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Spring's Model interface (a data carrier) with the conceptual Model layer in MVC architecture (services, repositories, business logic)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clearly differentiate Spring's Model object (view data container) from the MVC pattern's Model layer (business logic) and explain how Model isn't needed in REST controllers because @RestController serializes return values directly to JSON

sections.title: The Model Used for Server-rendered Views
sections.content:
Model attributes can also be supplied by @ModelAttribute methods and can participate in data binding. The model exists for view rendering; it is not a replacement for service-layer domain objects.

A well-separated MVC flow is controller -> service -> model attributes -> view. A REST flow is controller -> service -> response DTO -> message converter. The same DispatcherServlet can support both.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Model carries named attributes to a rendered view.
ModelMap and ModelAndView are related MVC options.
REST response objects are serialized return values, not the MVC Model container.
Domain model is a broader design term and should not be confused with org.springframework.ui.Model.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A page controller can call model.addAttribute("user", userDto) and return "profile". A Thymeleaf template then reads ${user.name}. For an API, returning userDto from a RestController skips view resolution and writes a response representation. Both objects contain data, but only the first uses Spring's Model abstraction. Keeping the terms separate makes the request flow easier to understand.

sections.title: The Model in Spring MVC
sections.content:
amber|Model|~Controller-to-view bag|model.addAttribute()|key-value data|server-side rendering
blue|In the view|~Read by the template|${userName} in Thymeleaf|renders dynamic HTML|MVC only
emerald|@RestController|~No Model needed|return the object|serialized to JSON|client renders it
rose|Trap|~Using Model in REST|JSON APIs ignore it|return a DTO instead|Model is for HTML

sections.title: Using Model in Traditional MVC vs REST
When to Use Spring's Model
sections.content:
Use the **Model interface** when building traditional server-side rendered applications with Thymeleaf, JSP, or Freemarker templates. If your controller returns a view name (String) and you need to pass data to that view, inject Model as a method parameter and add attributes.

Use **ModelAndView** when you want to set both the view name and model attributes in one object. For **REST APIs** returning JSON or XML, skip Model entirely — just return your domain objects or DTOs from `@RestController` methods. Spring's HttpMessageConverter will serialize them automatically.

Use **RedirectAttributes** (a Model subtype) when redirecting and need to pass flash attributes that survive the redirect.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using Model in REST controllers**: Freshers add Model parameters to `@RestController` methods thinking they need it for JSON responses. Spring REST doesn't use views, so Model attributes are ignored — just return the object directly.
- **Confusing Model with Model layer**: Saying "the Model handles business logic" mixes Spring's Model interface with the MVC architectural pattern's Model layer (services/entities). Spring's Model is just a data container.
- **Overloading Model with services**: Adding service objects to Model instead of the data they produce. The view needs data (a User object), not the UserService itself. Pass `model.addAttribute("user", userService.getUser())`, not the service.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: There are two things called Model in Spring MVC — one is the interface you inject, the other is the conceptual layer in the pattern. They're not the same thing.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: The conceptual M in MVC refers to the whole business layer — your entities, services, and repositories. That's the domain model.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: Spring's Model interface is something else entirely. It's a map you inject into a @Controller method to pass data to a view template. You call addAttribute with a key and a value, and the Thymeleaf template reads those values.

beats.label: differences
beats.content: For REST APIs using @RestController, you don't use the Model interface at all. You just return a Java object and Jackson serializes it to JSON. The Model object only exists in the traditional server-rendered MVC flow.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: Use the Model interface when building server-rendered pages with Thymeleaf. Use a plain return value when building REST APIs. ModelAndView is an older style that combines both the view name and the model data in one return object.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: candidates miss: @ModelAttribute has two distinct uses — on a method it populates a model attribute before every request handler in the class, on a parameter it binds form data to a Java object. Interviewers sometimes ask about both in the same question.

speakable_v2.cap: If you're asked about the Model in Spring MVC, clarify which one — the interface for view data, or the M in MVC meaning the domain layer.

question: What is the difference between Spring MVC and Spring REST?
title: Spring MVC vs Spring REST — View-Based vs API-Based
direct_answer: 'Spring REST' is not a separate framework from Spring MVC. Spring MVC can render server-side views or write response bodies for HTTP APIs. @Controller and @RestController are common choices, but either style can return ResponseEntity and a @Controller method can add @ResponseBody. The real difference is return-value handling and the endpoint contract, not an absolute controller annotation split.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Spring REST is built on Spring MVC architecture, not a separate framework, and knowing when to use each approach
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Spring REST is a different framework or module — it's just Spring MVC with @ResponseBody on every method, returning data instead of views
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @RestController is syntactic sugar for @Controller plus @ResponseBody, and both use the same DispatcherServlet — the only difference is response handling (view rendering vs JSON serialization)

sections.title: Spring REST APIs Use Spring MVC Infrastructure
sections.content:
Content negotiation can choose among supported representations, and ResponseEntity can control status and headers in either controller style. A REST API can even return HTML or a file representation when its contract supports that media type.

Use separate controller classes when view and API concerns would otherwise make return semantics confusing. The infrastructure remains Spring MVC.

**Example.** A browser page method can return "orders/list" with a Model for template rendering. An API method under @RestController can return List<OrderResponse>, which Jackson normally serializes to JSON. Both use Spring MVC's request mapping infrastructure.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: View flow: model attributes plus a resolved template/view.
API flow: response body written by an HttpMessageConverter.
Both use DispatcherServlet, mappings, argument resolution, validation, and exception handling.
One application can support both page and API endpoints.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A @Controller method returning "orders" can render templates/orders.html through a ViewResolver. Another @Controller method annotated @ResponseBody can return OrderDto as JSON. @RestController simply applies response-body behavior to all its handler methods. This makes it convenient for API-focused classes but does not create a different Spring web stack.

sections.title: Spring MVC vs Spring REST
sections.content:
amber|Spring MVC (web)|~Returns view names|renders HTML via Thymeleaf|server-side pages|@Controller
blue|Spring REST|~Returns data|object to JSON/XML|consumed by JS/mobile|@RestController
emerald|Same engine|~Both use DispatcherServlet|same HandlerMapping|differ only in output|@ResponseBody is the switch
violet|When to pick|~MVC for server pages|REST for APIs|REST dominates today|microservices + SPAs

sections.title: MVC vs REST Side-by-Side
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **Spring MVC (traditional)** when building server-side rendered applications where the backend generates complete HTML pages — think admin dashboards, content management systems, or classic monolithic web apps where each page load is a full server round-trip. It's great when you need SEO-friendly pages or rapid prototyping with templates.

Use **Spring REST** when building APIs that serve data to client-side JavaScript frameworks (React, Angular, Vue), mobile apps (iOS, Android), or other backend services. REST is the standard for microservices architectures and single-page applications where the frontend handles rendering. In practice, many applications use **both**: REST endpoints for dynamic features and AJAX calls, plus a few MVC endpoints for initial page loads or admin sections. If you're building a modern web app in 2024, you'll likely start with REST and add MVC only if you need server-rendered pages.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking they're separate frameworks**: Freshers believe Spring REST is a different module or framework from Spring MVC. They're the same — @RestController is just syntactic sugar for @Controller with @ResponseBody on every method. Both use DispatcherServlet.
- **Returning view names from @RestController**: Writing `return "user-list";` in a RestController method and expecting JSON. RestController treats String returns as literal response body, not view names. You'll get the string "user-list" as plain text, not JSON.
- **Mixing concerns**: Adding Model parameters to RestController methods or returning ResponseEntity from @Controller methods without @ResponseBody. If you need JSON, use @RestController. If you need views, use @Controller. Don't mix unless you explicitly use @ResponseBody on specific methods.

seo.metaTitle: Spring MVC vs Spring REST | Java Backend Fresher Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn the difference between Spring MVC and Spring REST — @Controller vs @RestController, HTML view vs JSON response, same DispatcherServlet infrastructure.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: Spring REST isn't a different framework — it's Spring MVC with the view layer removed and Jackson plugged in instead.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: Traditional Spring MVC uses @Controller to return view names. The server renders complete HTML pages using Thymeleaf or JSP and sends them to the browser. The browser just displays what it gets.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: Spring REST uses @RestController to return data objects. Jackson serializes them to JSON. The client — a browser running React, a mobile app, or another microservice — receives raw data and decides how to render it.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: Most modern Spring Boot apps are REST-only with a separate React or Angular frontend. But a single app can have both — @Controller routes for server-rendered admin pages and @RestController routes under /api for the mobile client.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: gotcha: Both approaches go through the same DispatcherServlet pipeline. Saying Spring REST uses a different request-handling infrastructure is incorrect — it doesn't.

speakable_v2.cap: Same DispatcherServlet, same HandlerMapping, same routing machinery. The only fork in the road is whether you hit a ViewResolver or an HttpMessageConverter.
